title: Liquid oxygen is pale blue and sticks to a magnet
body: Chill oxygen below −183 °C and it condenses into a liquid with a light sky-blue colour. Pour it between the poles of a strong magnet and it clings there as a bridge, because the O₂ molecule carries **two unpaired electrons** whose spins make it paramagnetic, attracted into magnetic fields. Simple dot-and-line pictures of bonding predict that all of oxygen’s electrons should be paired up; molecular orbital theory, which builds orbitals spanning the whole molecule, explains why two are left alone. The gas that makes up about 21% of the air you breathe is quietly magnetic.

slides.label: where oxygen condenses into a sky-blue liquid
slides.text: It freezes into a pale blue solid at about −219 °C.

slides.heading: A lab demonstration
items: Pour liquid oxygen between the poles of a strong magnet
It sticks, forming a bridge of liquid between the poles
The bridge holds until the liquid warms and boils away

slides.heading: Why oxygen is magnetic
slides.text: Electrons spin, and a spinning charge is a tiny magnet. In most molecules electrons pair up with opposite spins and cancel out. The O₂ molecule keeps two electrons unpaired, so each molecule is a little magnet that a field can pull on. That is paramagnetism: attraction without being a permanent magnet.

slides.question: What gives liquid oxygen its pull toward a magnet?
slides.explanation: Each O₂ molecule carries two unpaired electrons whose spins act as tiny magnets, so the liquid is drawn into a magnetic field.
